Vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the field. I can hear them under the soil, and I can strike from the branch. They are fat and juicy. I eat them whole, bones and all. The meadow voles are the best.

Voles. Small, soft, and easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the thump. I drop from the branch and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and numerous. I can hear them under the leaves and strike fast. They are the mainstay of my winter food. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit. But voles are best. They are everywhere and always there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow, under the willow, in the dry grass. They squeak and twitch, and I strike with my feet. One voles a night is enough. I don't like mice. They are too quick. And I never eat shrews. They are too small and too sharp.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run through the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I pounce, they squeak. They are good for a quick meal. Vole. They are small, soft, and full of fat. I can hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I can strike with precision. When I catch one, it's a feast. I eat the body, then I swallow the bones later. Voles are the best.

I prefer voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but I don't like the smell of them. The voles are better. I can hear them through the snow too, when it's quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I see the rustle of a vole in the long grass and drop. The grass is too thick for me to see the vole, but I can hear it. I wait for it to move, then drop.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. I listen for the sound of their scratching and then pounce. The grass is soft and hides them well. I have to be careful not to make too much noise. Mice. I hear them in the grass, and I drop from the ivy. I go in the dark, I go in the rain. I catch them with my talons. I eat them whole. I have a hollow in the willow for my pellets.

Mice. I can hear them moving through the grass. I sit still, listen, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down. I don't like the long grass. It is too soft and too tall. I prefer the meadow, the stream bank, the lane. I hunt in the dark. I hunt in the silence. I hunt in the dark.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, as I do my own eggs.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I eat in pieces. I can't swallow a whole rabbit. The rest I leave in the hollow.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. The bones come out later, when I regurgitate them. I know the shape of a vole's skull by now. I swallow the whole thing, skin and all.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small and soft, so I can eat them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything. I swallow the whole vole, bones and all. It is the way of owls. I do not chew. I do not swallow anything else whole. I swallow the whole vole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and digest them later. I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. The big ones I tear into pieces with my beak and claws. I eat them whole, though. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can crunch them in my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. I swallow the whole vole, bones and all. It is the way of owls. I do not like the taste of bones, but I do not refuse them. I swallow them whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole. It's the way it is. I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I tear them with my teeth and swallow them whole, head first. I don't chew. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I can't digest. I just swallow. It's the way I am. I don't know what it feels like to chew. I don't know what it feels like to taste. I just swallow.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, soft, and fit in my throat. I chew them a little, but mostly I swallow them whole. Voles. Small and fat. I can hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I can hear them squeak when I strike. They are the most common in the meadow.

Voles. I catch them in the meadow at dusk. I sit on the fence post and wait. They come out to feed. I strike with my talons. I eat them whole. They are soft and juicy. I do not like shrews. They are too small and have too many teeth.
Voles. Small, brown, and soft. They run in the meadow, and I sit still and wait for the scent to come to me. I fly down and catch them with my feet. I do not like the smell of their bodies.
Voles. I hear them rustling in the dry grass and the undergrowth. I catch them with a quick dive from the branch.

Voles. Vole and mouse are the same to me. I hear them moving in the dry grass and I drop from the branch. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole.
Voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit still in the ivy. I hear them scratching under the leaves and snap down. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole.
A vole. I catch voles in the grass. I sit still and wait for one to pop up, then I drop. I can hear them in the grass, and I can see them in the snow. I catch them with my feet. They are not quick.
Voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them with a quick dive. I can hear them under the leaves. I don't like them, but they're easy. I catch more voles than any other.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch for owls or foxes or badgers. My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have a nest there, and I have raised my owlets. My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dry and deep, and it holds me through the long cold. I sit there and listen. I do not go far. I have a mate, and we have our young. We are together. I do not go far. I do not go far.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. Inside, it is dark and warm. I have a nest of feathers and a few pellets. My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is dark and dry, and I have a nest of feathers and a few dead voles. I sit in it when it is dark, and I call. The hollow is warm, and the wind does not reach it. I do not leave it unless I must hunt. I return when the moon is full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and deep, and the stream is a mile away. I can hear it in the night. I can hear the water running. I can hear the fish.

A hollow in the old willow. The bark is rough, the leaves dry. I have nested there for three years. My mate and I raise our young there. The wind comes through the branches, and the owlets call from the hollow. I do not speak of it. I am there.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. I have lived there for years. It is dark and dry and warm in the winter. I do not leave it often. I fly to the meadow to hunt, but I always return. A hollow in the old willow, right where the lane bends. The ivy grows thick and the bark is soft, so I can sleep without being jostled. I have a nest in the hollow, and I have a mate. I do not know the word for home, but I know it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old willow. It is a dry hollow, just wide enough for me to turn in, and high enough to keep the wind out. I have been there all my life, and I will be there when I die. I do not know what it is like to live elsewhere. The willow is my world.

It is the hollow in the old willow by the stream. I have been there for many winters. The stream runs cold, and the willow is solid and deep. A hollow in the old willow. I sit in it all through the night, and I scratch the bark with my claws. I have a mate in the hollow too, and we have a hollow for our young. The willow is near the stream, and the stream is near the lane. I can hear the lane from my hollow.
